actions.justification: Mandatory first step - patient has tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, and hypoxia requiring formal vital signs assessment to establish baseline severity.
Mandatory - SpO2 of 91% and RR of 24 indicate significant respiratory compromise; formal respiratory assessment needed to determine need for supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support.
Mandatory - chest radiography required per ATS/IDSA guidelines to confirm diagnosis of pneumonia and characterize the RLL consolidation.
MANDATORY action per guidelines and required within 60 minutes. CBC will assess WBC count, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, all relevant to severity assessment and diagnosis of pneumonia.

ATS/IDSA CAP guidelines recommend CURB-65 scoring to stratify pneumonia severity and guide site-of-care decisions (outpatient, inpatient, or ICU). This patient has tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, and hypoxia suggesting moderate-to-severe disease.

Blood cultures should be obtained BEFORE antibiotic administration per ATS/IDSA CAP guidelines. This patient has signs of systemic infection (fever, tachycardia, tachypnea) and aspiration pneumonia risk factors, making bacteremia possible.

Patient has SpO2 91%, RR 24, HR 100 — meeting potential minor criteria for severe CAP (hypoxemia, tachypnea, tachycardia). ICU criteria assessment is critical to determine if escalation is needed per ATS/IDSA guidelines.

Aspiration pneumonia with foul-smelling sputum strongly suggests polymicrobial/anaerobic infection. Sputum culture is essential to identify causative organisms and guide targeted antibiotic therapy, especially given poor dentition and alcohol use.
BMP is needed to assess renal function (drug dosing), electrolytes (alcohol use risk for hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia), glucose, and BUN (part of CURB-65 urea component and overall metabolic status).

Procalcitonin helps assess severity of bacterial infection and can guide antibiotic therapy decisions in pneumonia. Patient has signs of significant infection (temp 38.8, HR 100, RR 24, SpO2 91%) making this a useful inflammatory marker.

ATS/IDSA guidelines recommend prompt antibiotic administration for CAP. This patient has aspiration pneumonia with concerning vitals (SpO2 91%, RR 24, temp 38.8°C) and risk factors (alcohol use, poor dentition). Beta-lactam plus macrolide is first-line for CAP/aspiration pneumonia. Blood cultures already obtained so antibiotics should not be delayed further.

Patient has tachycardia (HR 100), elevated RR (24), and SpO2 of 91% consistent with significant physiologic stress from pneumonia. IV fluid resuscitation is indicated to support hemodynamics and tissue perfusion. MAP of 86 is acceptable but trending is needed.

Patient has severe CAP features (SpO2 91%, RR 24, fever, found down with alcohol use) — Legionella urinary antigen is recommended by ATS/IDSA guidelines for hospitalized CAP patients, especially those with severe presentation or risk factors like alcohol use. This is a quick, non-invasive test that can guide targeted therapy.

Patient has aspiration pneumonia with poor dentition, chronic alcohol use, and signs of severity (SpO2 91%, HR 100, RR 24, Temp 38.8°C). Beta-lactam plus macrolide has already been given; adding or switching to a respiratory fluoroquinolone (e.g., levofloxacin) provides broader anaerobic and atypical coverage appropriate for aspiration pneumonia. Note: QT interval should be monitored given fluoroquinolone use.

Patient has SpO2 of 91% which is below the target threshold of ≥94%. Supplemental oxygen is immediately indicated to correct hypoxemia in this aspiration pneumonia patient with RR of 24 and signs of respiratory distress.

Patient was found down with chronic alcohol use. Mental status assessment is critical for CURB-65 scoring (confusion component), aspiration risk stratification, and airway protection evaluation. Altered mental status may necessitate intubation.
